drug_name: Estriol, Estradiol, Progesterone, and DHEA (Compounded Hormone Combination)
what_its_for: This combination of hormones is used to help relieve symptoms of menopause or hormone imbalance in women. It may help reduce hot flashes, night sweats, mood swings, vaginal dryness, low sex drive, fatigue, and trouble sleeping. Estriol and estradiol are forms of estrogen that help balance hormone levels. Progesterone helps protect the uterus and can support mood and sleep. DHEA is a natural hormone that your body uses to make estrogen and testosterone, and it can help with energy, mood, and sexual function. This medication is usually made specifically for you at a compounding pharmacy based on your doctor's prescription.
how_to_take: This medication may come as a cream, gel, capsule, tablet, troche (a lozenge you dissolve in your mouth), or vaginal insert depending on your prescription. Follow your doctor's specific instructions carefully. If using a cream or gel, apply it to clean, dry skin on areas such as the inner wrist, inner arm, or inner thigh — wherever your doctor tells you. Rotate application sites each day to avoid skin irritation. Do not apply to broken, irritated, or oily skin. If taking a capsule or troche, take it exactly as directed, usually at bedtime. Wash your hands before and after applying a cream or gel. Never share this medication with anyone else.
dosing: Your dose is specially made for you and will be written on your prescription label. Dosing varies widely from person to person based on your hormone levels and symptoms. A typical starting dose for creams might be a small measured amount (such as 0.25 to 1 gram) applied once or twice daily. Capsules may be taken once daily, often at bedtime. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on how you feel and follow-up blood or saliva hormone tests. Always use the measuring device (pump, syringe, or dosing card) provided with your medication to get the correct amount. Do not increase or decrease your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it or apply it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is already the next day, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or use two doses at once to make up for a missed one. If you miss several doses in a row, contact your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store this medication at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C), unless your pharmacist gives you different instructions. Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the cap tightly closed when not in use. Keep out of reach of children and pets — accidental exposure to hormone cream can affect children, men, and animals. Check the expiration date on your prescription label and do not use it after that date. If you have any leftover medication, ask your pharmacist about safe disposal options.
what_to_avoid: Avoid applying hormone cream to areas where others may come into contact with your skin, such as the neck or chest, to prevent accidental transfer to a partner, child, or pet. Avoid letting others touch the area where you applied the cream until it is fully absorbed (usually 2 to 5 minutes). Avoid smoking while using hormone therapy, as it increases the risk of serious side effects such as blood clots. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice unless your doctor says it is okay, as it may affect how your body processes estrogen. Avoid taking extra herbal hormones, soy supplements, or over-the-counter hormone products without asking your doctor first. Do not apply cream or gel to irritated, sunburned, or broken skin.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden chest pain, shortness of breath, or coughing up blood (which could be a sign of a blood clot); sudden severe headache, vision changes, weakness, or trouble speaking (signs of possible stroke); pain, swelling, or redness in one leg (sign of a possible blood clot in the leg); unusual vaginal bleeding or spotting, especially if you have not had a period in a year or more; a lump in your breast or changes in your breast; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); severe skin rash or allergic reaction; signs of depression, unusual mood changes, or thoughts of harming yourself; swelling of the hands, feet, or ankles that is new or getting worse. Also call your doctor if your symptoms are not improving after a few weeks, or if you have any new or bothersome side effects.
when_it_works: Most women begin to notice some improvement in symptoms like hot flashes, sleep problems, and mood within 2 to 4 weeks of starting treatment. Vaginal dryness and sexual symptoms may take 4 to 12 weeks to improve. Full benefit from hormone therapy may take 2 to 3 months. Your doctor will check your hormone levels and adjust your dose as needed. Keep all follow-up appointments so your doctor can make sure the treatment is working safely for you.
special_populations: Older women (over 65): Use with caution. The risk of blood clots, stroke, and certain cancers may be higher in older women. Your doctor will use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time needed. Women with a uterus: Progesterone is included in this combination to help protect the lining of the uterus from overgrowth (endometrial hyperplasia) caused by estrogen. Do not skip the progesterone portion of your treatment. Women with a history of breast cancer, uterine cancer, blood clots, liver disease, or stroke: This combination may not be safe for you. Be sure to tell your doctor your full medical history before starting. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do NOT use hormone therapy if you are pregnant, trying to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. These hormones can harm a developing baby and may pass into breast milk. Women with thyroid conditions or diabetes: Hormone therapy may affect your thyroid hormone levels and blood sugar. Your doctor may need to monitor and adjust your other medications.
